title: Who I am
job: Introduce yourself and state what you like
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A Korean sentence puts its verb LAST, every time. Jeo-neun haksaeng-ieyo is, piece by piece, 'I-topic student-am'. Nothing moves it and nothing follows it, so once you know the last word of a sentence you know what is being done.

Small endings called particles mark what each word is DOING in the sentence — the topic, the subject, the object. Because the particle carries the job, the order of the words in front of the verb is about emphasis, not grammar. This course writes those endings with a hyphen — jeo-neun, keopi-reul — so you can see the seam. Korean itself writes them joined straight onto the word, with no hyphen and no space; the hyphen is a teaching mark, not part of the spelling.

'Am', 'is' and 'are' are not a separate word. The copula attaches to the noun: -ieyo after a consonant (haksaeng-ieyo), -yeyo after a vowel (uisa-yeyo). One ending, both jobs, and it is the last thing in the sentence because it is the verb.

-neun (after a vowel) and -eun (after a consonant) mark the TOPIC — what the sentence is about. Introductions take it: jeo-neun, je ireum-eun, je chingu-neun. It is one ending in two shapes, chosen by the sound in front of it, exactly like the copula.

-i (after a consonant) and -ga (after a vowel) mark the SUBJECT — what is new, or singled out, or the thing being denied. The honest rule at this stage is that a topic is what you are talking about and a subject is what you are pointing at; the rest comes with hearing it.

There are no articles at all. chaek is 'book', 'a book' and 'the book' — nothing on the page tells them apart, and nothing needs to. There is no plural marking either in ordinary speech: chaek is 'books' too when the situation says so.

joahaeyo ('like') is a VERB and it takes an object, marked with -eul after a consonant and -reul after a vowel: keopi-reul joahaeyo, chaek-eul joahaeyo. English 'like' behaves the same way, so the only new thing is that the object wears its marker and the verb waits at the end.

You cannot negate the copula by putting a word in front of it. 'Is not' is its own word, anieyo, and what it denies takes -i/-ga rather than the topic marker: jeo-neun seonsaengnim-i anieyo. There is no shape of -ieyo that means 'is not'.

This course speaks the -yo style — what you use with anyone you have just met, a shopkeeper, a colleague, an official. That decides the word for 'I': jeo, and its possessive je. The other word for 'I' belongs to the style you use with close friends, and it is not taught here.

Possession needs no word at all when one noun simply sits in front of another: je chingu is 'my friend', je chingu ireum is 'my friend's name'. Stack them and read left to right, exactly as English does with 'my friend's name'.

sentences.trap: There is no word for 'a' to put in front of haksaeng, and no word for 'am' to put in the middle. If you are hunting for either one you are hunting for something Korean does not have.
sentences.sound: juh-nun HAK-ssaeng-ee-eh-yo. The eo of jeo is the vowel in English 'nut', not the one in 'no' — that difference is real and it separates words. In haksaeng the s tenses after the k, so it comes out hak-ssaeng, and the whole thing runs on into -ieyo with no break: the ending is part of the word, and it is said that way.

mistake.why: Two markers cannot sit on the same word, and the copula cannot leave the noun it belongs to. -eun marks ireum as the topic; -yeyo belongs on Minsu, at the end, where the verb goes.

The k at the end of hanguk is held, not released — the mouth closes on it and stops, and English speakers tend to add a little puff of air that is not there. saram has two even, light syllables; neither is stressed, because Korean does not stress one syllable over another the way English does.

mistake.why: That says 'I am Korea' — the country itself. The person needs saram: hanguk saram, a Korea-person. This is one of the few places where dropping a word changes the sentence into something absurd rather than merely wrong.

'Coffee' — borrowed from English and reshaped to fit Korean sounds, which is why it has three syllables. With -reul it is the thing you like or drink; with -yeyo it is what something is.
The object marker, in two shapes: -eul after a consonant (chaek-eul), -reul after a vowel (keopi-reul). It marks what the verb acts on, which English does by position — so the object can move.
'Like' — a verb that takes an object: keopi-reul joahaeyo. Not joayo, which comes later and means 'is good': that describes the thing itself and takes no object. Same root, two jobs.

sentences.trap: English puts the verb in the middle, and everything in you will want to say 'I like — coffee'. Korean puts the object first, wearing its marker, and holds the verb to the end. The marker is what tells you coffee is the thing being liked, so nothing is lost by the wait.
sentences.sound: juh-nun KUH-pee-rul jo-ah-HAE-yo. keopi has the same eo as jeo, so it is 'kuh', not 'ko'. joahaeyo has an h buried in the middle of the written word that nobody pronounces — it runs together as jo-a-hae-yo, which is exactly what this course writes, because this course spells words the way they are said.

mistake.why: The verb has been dragged into the middle, English-style, and the object has been left bare at the end. Korean never does either: the object wears -reul and the verb finishes the sentence.
